records.title: Islam and the four principles of medical ethics.
records.design: Conceptual/theoretical analysis (non-empirical bioethics scholarship)
records.population_setting: General Muslim patient population; clinician-facing framework, no primary cohort
records.key_finding: Maps the Beauchamp-Childress four principles (beneficence, nonmaleficence, justice, autonomy) onto Islamic ethical-legal reasoning, arguing each principle has an identifiable root in Islamic jurisprudence, and that clinicians who understand this achieve more culturally concordant consultations.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Positions 'adl (justice) and the harm-avoidance (nonmaleficence) safeguard as bridgeable to mainstream biomedical-ethics language, which is exactly the pairing T-PHE needs between its Islamic frame and medical science. Supports T-PHE's premise that an Islamic ethical vocabulary can sit alongside, not against, standard clinical-ethics principles for the informed-consent/autonomy safeguard.
records.evidence_level: Tier one by explicit journal inclusion — Journal of Medical Ethics (flagship specialty bioethics journal named in the search brief) regardless of article design.

records.title: Muslim patients and cross-gender interactions in medicine: an Islamic bioethical perspective.
records.design: Bioethical/ethico-legal analysis with clinical vignette
records.population_setting: Muslim patients in cross-gender clinical encounters (dress code, seclusion, physical contact); US/Western clinical settings
records.key_finding: Develops an Islamic bioethical framework for gender-boundary norms in the patient-provider relationship, arguing religion functions as a 'cultural repertoire' shaping consent and comfort, and offers ethico-legal guidance for accommodating these norms without compromising care quality.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Positions amanah (entrusted responsibility of the provider/educator to respect boundaries) and consent as gender- and modesty-sensitive constructs, not generic autonomy — directly relevant to how T-PHE frames premarital counseling delivery (mixed-gender facilitation, physical-examination content). Supports the safeguard that consent processes must be adapted to Islamic gender-interaction norms rather than assumed universal.
records.evidence_level: Tier one by explicit journal inclusion — Journal of Medical Ethics.

records.title: Moral universe of Muslim healthcare practitioners in the UK: balancing Islamic and secular ethics in palliative and end-of-life care.
records.design: Qualitative study, 76 semi-structured interviews (Muslim patients, family members, Muslim and non-Muslim palliative-care providers)
records.population_setting: Muslim healthcare practitioners and patients/families in UK palliative and end-of-life care (NHS)
records.key_finding: Muslim HCPs experience significant moral distress reconciling Islamic moral frameworks with NHS secular ethics; the study identifies gaps in institutional ethical-support systems and recommends religious-competence training and peer-support structures for religious clinicians.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Positions amanah (professional trust/entrusted duty) empirically: it documents the real strain when an Islamic ethical frame is not scaffolded institutionally, which complicates T-PHE's assumption that declaring an Islamic frame is sufficient — it is analogous evidence that faith-frame-vs-secular-system tension is a real, measurable phenomenon among Muslim health professionals, an important caution for anyone delivering T-PHE inside a non-Islamic health system.
records.evidence_level: Tier one by explicit journal inclusion — Journal of Medical Ethics.

records.title: Islamic medical ethics: a primer.
records.design: Narrative review/primer
records.population_setting: General overview of Islamic medical ethics literature; no specific population
records.key_finding: Surveys the scope of Islamic Medical Ethics scholarship from virtue-based character development to Islamic-law-derived rulings, covering abortion, gender relations in the patient-doctor relationship, and end-of-life care, aiming to give clinicians and ethicists a working overview of the Islamic paradigm.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Foundational tier-one text positioning the overall Islamic ethics vocabulary (encompassing taqwa-grounded character formation and amanah-grounded law-derived rulings) that T-PHE's five-term frame (faqr/taqwa/amanah/'adl/shura) draws from. Supports T-PHE's basic premise that a distinct, citable Islamic Medical Ethics literature exists to pair with medical science, without itself validating T-PHE's programme.
records.evidence_level: Tier one by explicit journal inclusion — Bioethics (flagship specialty journal named in the search brief).

records.title: Islamic views on artificial nutrition and hydration in terminally ill patients.
records.design: Ethico-legal analysis
records.population_setting: Terminally ill Muslim patients; end-of-life decision-making
records.key_finding: Islamic law permits withdrawal of futile, harm-causing artificial nutrition/hydration but forbids deliberately hastening death; the decision is framed as a shared one involving patient, family, providers, and religious scholars, anchored in the harm-avoidance principle.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Concrete worked example of harm-avoidance ('adl-adjacent nonmaleficence) and consultative (shura-like) multi-party decision-making — patient + family + clinician + scholar — that T-PHE's shura safeguard can cite as precedent for how Islamic ethics operationalizes consultation in a medical decision, even though the clinical topic (end-of-life) differs from premarital health education.
records.evidence_level: Tier one by explicit journal inclusion — Bioethics.

records.title: Bioethics for clinicians: 21. Islamic bioethics.
records.design: Narrative overview (clinician education series)
records.population_setting: General Muslim patient population in a Western (Canadian) clinical context
records.key_finding: Summarizes Islamic bioethics as a combination of revelation-derived principles, duties, rights and virtue; stresses prevention, respect, compassion, and attention to physical/mental/spiritual dimensions of illness, while cautioning against a stereotyped, homogenous view of 'the Muslim patient.'
records.relevance_to_tphe: A leading general-medicine journal's own primer supports the legitimacy of citing an Islamic ethical frame (faqr/taqwa/amanah as spiritual-dimension-of-illness concepts) in mainstream clinical literature; its explicit warning against treating Muslim patients as a monolith is a needed complicating note for T-PHE, which must not present its five-term frame as uniformly authoritative across all Muslim communities in Thailand.
records.evidence_level: Tier one by explicit journal inclusion — CMAJ is a leading, long-established national general-medical journal, though not conventionally ranked alongside the NEJM/Lancet/JAMA/BMJ 'big-4' by impact factor/citation standing [corrected 2026-09-02: original claim of direct Lancet/BMJ/JAMA-tier equivalence was an overclaim].

records.title: Faith-Based Lifestyle Intervention for Diabetes Prevention Among Adults in Bangladesh: A Cluster Randomized Clinical Trial.
records.design: Cluster-randomized controlled trial, 8 mosque clusters, 5 districts, 12-month follow-up
records.population_setting: Adults aged 25-65 with prediabetes, rural Bangladesh, mosque-based delivery by imams and trained female assistants
records.key_finding: A 12-month mosque-based, faith-integrated lifestyle intervention (Islamic teachings plus diet/activity/behavior-change guidance delivered by imams and trained female assistants) significantly reduced 12-month cumulative type 2 diabetes incidence versus usual care among adults with prediabetes in rural Bangladesh: intervention 9.8% (95% CI 7.1-13.5%) vs control 17.1% (95% CI 13.4-21.6%); absolute risk reduction 7.3 percentage points (95% CI 5.2-10.6); relative risk reduction 42.5% (95% CI 15.0-70.0%); number needed to treat 14 (95% CI 9-39); adjusted hazard ratio 0.75 (95% CI 0.60-0.95, P=.02). Secondary metabolic/behavioral outcomes (weight, BMI, glycemic markers, lipids, blood pressure, knowledge, activity, quality of life) also improved significantly more in the intervention arm. [Corrected 2026-09-02: the original key_finding wrongly claimed these effect sizes were truncated in the fetched record — the full PubMed abstract contains complete numeric results, reproduced above.]
records.relevance_to_tphe: Directly analogous delivery model — using mosque infrastructure and trusted faith leaders (an amanah-consistent delivery channel) to carry a structured health-behavior curriculum — is the closest real-world RCT precedent for T-PHE's own mosque/community-based premarital education delivery. Supports feasibility of faith-integrated health curricula delivered by trained lay/religious facilitators; does not itself test premarital health content, so it is an analogy on delivery channel, not outcome content.
records.evidence_level: Tier one by explicit journal inclusion — JAMA Network Open (JAMA family) plus RCT design.

records.title: Lay-Led Intervention for War and Refugee Trauma: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
records.design: Randomized clinical trial, n=101, mosque-based and virtual delivery, 12-week follow-up
records.population_setting: US-based Somali refugees with DSM-5 Criterion A trauma exposure and PTSD symptoms, Seattle WA and Columbus OH
records.key_finding: Islamic Trauma Healing (ITH) — a brief, lay-led, mosque-based intervention combining psychoeducation, narratives of prophetic trauma, and prayer-integrated cognitive-behavioral techniques — significantly outperformed a waitlist control among 101 US-based Somali refugees with PTSD symptoms (intention-to-treat analysis) on PTSD severity (Cohen's d=-0.67), depression (d=-0.66), and well-being (d=0.71) at post-intervention, with gains maintained through 12-week follow-up. [Corrected 2026-09-02: the original key_finding wrongly claimed these effect sizes were truncated in the fetched abstract — the full PubMed abstract contains complete Cohen's-d results, reproduced above.] NOTE: two published errata exist (JAMA Netw Open 2024;7(9):e2440198 and 2024;7(10):e2446257); the effect sizes quoted here must be re-checked against the corrected article before citation.
records.relevance_to_tphe: A rare RCT-grade example of a faith-sensitive, Islamically-integrated psychotherapy delivered by lay community (mosque) leaders rather than clinicians — directly supports angle (d) that faith-integrated interventions among Muslim populations can be rigorously trialed, and models a taqwa-consistent (spiritually grounded coping) intervention design T-PHE could reference for its own faith-integrated counseling components.
records.evidence_level: Tier one by explicit journal inclusion — JAMA Network Open plus RCT design.

records.title: Exploring Cultural and Religious Effects on HPV Vaccination Decision Making Using a Web-Based Decision Aid: A Quasi-experimental Study.
records.design: Quasi-experimental study using a web-based shared-decision-making aid, Israeli parents/young adults stratified by religious group
records.population_setting: Israeli parents and young adults, stratified by religious group; the study population is majority Jewish (including ultra-Orthodox) but the abstract also reports a Muslim-Arab subgroup result [corrected 2026-09-02: original 'not a Muslim sample' description was inaccurate].
records.key_finding: In this quasi-experimental (non-randomized, pre/post questionnaire) study, a web-based decision aid significantly improved HPV vaccination intentions, knowledge, and decisional self-efficacy across most religious groups, but ultra-Orthodox Jewish participants exhibited persistent reluctance to vaccinate themselves or their children (OR=0.23, P<.001 for parents; OR=0.43, P<.001 for young adults) despite improved knowledge; by contrast, Muslim-Arab participants showed increased vaccination inclination (OR=3.12, P<.001) relative to comparison groups — showing generic decision-support tools do not work uniformly across all religiously conservative communities, and that a Muslim subgroup in this same dataset trended toward, not against, vaccination uptake. [Corrected 2026-09-02: the abstract does not state the reported odds ratios are covariate-adjusted, and the design is quasi-experimental rather than randomized, so the original 'adjusted OR' framing overstated the causal strength of this finding; the omitted Muslim-Arab subgroup result has also been added.]
records.relevance_to_tphe: Primarily an analogy (the reluctant subgroup is ultra-Orthodox Jewish, not Muslim): it demonstrates empirically that faith-sensitive, community-specific tailoring of shared-decision-making tools (T-PHE's shura/consultation safeguard) is necessary — a generic autonomy-based decision aid measurably underperforms in a theologically conservative community, complicating any assumption that standard health-education materials will transfer without adaptation to a religiously conservative Muslim audience. The study's own Muslim-Arab subgroup (OR=3.12 toward increased vaccination inclination) should also be cited directly — it is small, unadjusted, and not itself premarital-content evidence, but it is a same-study Muslim-population data point, not only cross-population analogy. [Corrected 2026-09-02 to add this subgroup finding, previously omitted.]
records.evidence_level: Tier one — Medical Decision Making is the official peer-reviewed journal of the Society for Medical Decision Making, a leading specialty journal for shared decision-making research.

records.title: Stressors, Needs and Satisfaction of Families of Critically Ill Arabic Patients: A Systematic Review.
records.design: Systematic review (PRISMA 2020), 52 studies, 2005-March 2025
records.population_setting: Families (Muslim and Christian) of critically ill Arabic patients in ICU settings
records.key_finding: 52 studies (58% high quality) show families' key stressors are uncertainty, restricted visitation, financial burden, and cultural/linguistic barriers; key needs are emotional reassurance, spiritual guidance, clear communication, and involvement in decision-making.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Systematic-review-grade evidence that family involvement in medical decision-making is a consistently identified need in Arabic/Muslim-adjacent populations — supports T-PHE's amanah/shura framing of family as a legitimate co-decision-maker rather than an intrusion on individual autonomy, though the clinical setting (ICU) differs from premarital counseling and must be treated as an analogy, not direct evidence.
records.evidence_level: Tier one — PRISMA systematic review.

records.title: Gender-Based Violence Against Migrant Women From Islamic Background: A Systematic Review of International Studies.
records.design: Systematic review (PRISMA), 25 studies from 332 screened, 2004-2024, mixed-methods appraisal tool
records.population_setting: Migrant women from Islamic-majority backgrounds, international (multi-country) settings
records.key_finding: Systematic review (PRISMA; 25 studies, 2004-2024) of gender-based violence among migrant women from Islamic backgrounds: intimate-partner violence was the most prevalent form, with female genital mutilation and forced marriage also reported. Risk and protective factors were identified across ecological levels: individual level - language barriers and lack of awareness of services (risk) vs spirituality and knowledge of rights (protective); microsystem - the husband's control over the woman's life and economic dependence (risk) vs concern for children and financial independence (protective); exosystem - the negative role of religious leaders (risk) vs support from assistance services (protective).
records.relevance_to_tphe: Complicates any reading of religion or family as uniformly protective: spirituality and knowledge of rights protect, but husband control and religious leaders' negative role are named risk factors - directly relevant to R1 (culture/religion must not close a safety question), R2 (private channel) and Layer 0 (knowledge of rights). Migrant populations in Europe/Spain-focused search; analogy for Thailand.
records.evidence_level: Tier one — PRISMA systematic review in a leading specialty journal on violence/abuse.

records.title: Factors influencing sexual and reproductive health of Muslim women: a systematic review.
records.design: Systematic review, narrative synthesis, 59 studies from 22 countries
records.population_setting: Muslim women worldwide; sexual and reproductive health (SRH) knowledge, attitudes, service access
records.key_finding: Many Muslim women have poor SRH knowledge and negative attitudes limiting SRH service/contraception use; husband and family opposition, religious/cultural beliefs, and fear of stigmatization (being perceived as having premarital sexual relations) were major barriers to accessing SRH services and information.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Directly on-topic tier-one systematic review: documents that stigma around premarital sexuality and family/husband gatekeeping are real, evidenced barriers to reproductive-health knowledge among Muslim women — this is strong supporting evidence for T-PHE's core premise that premarital health education fills a genuine, documented knowledge gap, while also complicating the 'family involvement is protective' framing by showing family opposition itself functions as a barrier that a faqr (limited-knowledge)-aware curriculum must address rather than assume away.
records.evidence_level: Tier one — systematic review (BioMed Central Reproductive Health, PubMed-indexed).

records.title: Assisted reproductive technology: Islamic Sunni perspective.
records.design: Systematic review of the literature, Medline search 1978-2013
records.population_setting: General Islamic Sunni jurisprudential literature on assisted reproductive technology
records.key_finding: Sunni Islamic law permits ART only within a legally married couple during an intact marriage, forbids all forms of surrogacy and third-party gamete/embryo donation, and permits gender selection only for medical reasons (with some jurists allowing limited social reasons).
records.relevance_to_tphe: Tier-one systematic review establishing that Islamic reproductive-decision boundaries are explicitly marriage-contract-bound (the marital dyad is the licit unit for reproductive decisions) — supports T-PHE's premise that premarital preparation (establishing a sound marital contract/relationship) is the ethically load-bearing gateway for later reproductive decision-making in Islamic law, an 'adl/justice-of-the-marital-contract framing.
records.evidence_level: Tier one — explicitly labeled systematic review of the literature.

records.title: Health Effects of Religion, Spirituality, and Supernatural Beliefs in Mainland China: A Systematic Review.
records.design: Bilingual (Chinese-English) systematic review, CASP quality appraisal, 162 studies of 1858 screened
records.population_setting: General mainland Chinese population (predominantly non-Muslim; folk religion, Buddhism, Christianity, some Islam)
records.key_finding: Religion/spirituality/supernatural-belief research on health in China grew from 5 to 73 studies per 5-year period 2000-2019, but only 7% of studies were higher quality; higher-quality studies showed both beneficial and adverse health implications of religious/spiritual belief, with fundamental evidence gaps remaining (mostly cross-sectional design, single-item religiosity measures).
records.relevance_to_tphe: Population differs sharply (mainland China, largely non-Muslim) so this is an analogy, not direct evidence, but as a tier-one systematic review it supports the general, cross-cultural finding that religiosity/spirituality has a real but methodologically under-evidenced (mostly cross-sectional, low measurement quality) relationship to health outcomes — a needed caution against over-claiming causal benefit for T-PHE's own faith-integrated design, consistent with the requirement never to claim T-PHE itself is effective.
records.evidence_level: Tier one — Journal of Religion and Health, explicitly labeled systematic review (meets the search brief's 'J Relig Health SRs' criterion).

records.title: The Relationship Between Religiosity and Anxiety: A Meta-analysis.
records.design: Meta-analysis of 10 Arabic-language studies
records.population_setting: Arab citizens, ages 14-43, vast majority Muslim, seven religiosity/anxiety scales
records.key_finding: All 10 study correlations between religiosity and anxiety were negative; mean effect size r = -0.22 (range -0.16 to -0.43), suggesting religiosity may buffer anxiety via coping mechanisms; age and gender did not significantly moderate the association.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Directly relevant tier-one meta-analysis for angle (c): quantifies a modest but consistent inverse association between religiosity and anxiety in a largely Muslim Arab sample, supporting (with appropriate effect-size caution, r≈-0.22 is a small-to-moderate correlation, not proof of causal benefit) the plausibility that taqwa-grounded religious coping could be protective for anxiety among the population T-PHE targets — must be cited as correlational coping evidence, not as validation of T-PHE's specific curriculum.
records.evidence_level: Tier one — Journal of Religion and Health, explicitly labeled meta-analysis (meets the search brief's 'J Relig Health SRs' criterion, meta-analysis is the equivalent higher tier).

records.title: Drivers and consequences of self-immolation in parts of Iran, Iraq and Uzbekistan: A systematic review of qualitative evidence.
records.design: Systematic review of qualitative studies, 7 of 236 screened papers, 5 databases
records.population_setting: Survivors, family, and health-care staff in parts of Iran, Iraq, and Uzbekistan (Islamic-majority Central/West Asian countries)
records.key_finding: Marital and familial conflict, male-dominated culture, mental-health disorders, and economic/social factors were the main drivers of self-immolation (a severe, often fatal self-harm method disproportionately used by women in this region); consequences included social isolation, regret, and lasting physical/psychological harm.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Tier-one systematic review that starkly complicates any romanticized framing of family/marital authority in these societies: it documents marital and familial conflict as a direct driver of catastrophic self-harm, which is strong justification for T-PHE's 'adl (justice) and harm-avoidance safeguards to explicitly address marital conflict-resolution and women's agency within premarital preparation, not merely family-consultation ritual.
records.evidence_level: Tier one — systematic review of qualitative evidence, leading specialty journal (Burns, official journal of the International Society for Burn Injuries).

records.title: Faith, fasting, and well-being: Emirates Neurology Society consensus guidelines on safe Ramadan fasting in Parkinson's disease.
records.design: Professional society consensus guideline (Emirates Neurology Society), synthesizing existing guidance (BIMA Ramadan Compendium) and specialist clinical expertise
records.population_setting: Muslim patients with Parkinson's disease considering Ramadan fasting, Middle Eastern and global Muslim populations
records.key_finding: Provides a stepwise, risk-stratified algorithm (by Hoehn and Yahr stage) for individualized pre-Ramadan risk assessment and medication-timing adjustment, distinguishing patients who can fast safely from those advised against fasting.
records.relevance_to_tphe: A worked example of a formal, professional-society consensus guideline that operationalizes an Islamic religious practice (fasting) safely within a specific clinical population — directly modeling the format T-PHE would need (angle g) if it seeks eventual FIMA/IMANA-style professional guideline status: individualized risk stratification plus religious-practice accommodation, rather than blanket permission or blanket restriction.
records.evidence_level: Tier one with a caveat — PubMed classifies this article as a narrative Review, not a formally tagged 'Practice Guideline'; it synthesizes an existing guideline (BIMA Ramadan Compendium), drug-pharmacokinetic literature, and a professional-society (Emirates Neurology Society) consensus meeting/expert opinion, which is consensus-level clinical guidance rather than itself a PubMed-classified formal guideline. Frontiers in Neurology is also a high-volume, broad-scope journal with more variable editorial selectivity than a dedicated movement-disorders specialty journal, so 'leading specialty journal' should not be read as top-tier. [Corrected 2026-09-02: original text overclaimed this as an 'explicit professional/clinical consensus guideline' in an unqualified 'leading specialty journal'; still usable as expert-consensus-level evidence for angle (g), downgraded accordingly.]

records.title: Informed consent with a focus on islamic views.
records.journal: The Journal of IMA (Islamic Medical Association of North America)
records.design: Narrative/conceptual analysis
records.population_setting: General discussion of informed consent for Muslim patients
records.key_finding: Traces informed consent's shift from a purely autonomy-based principle toward a shared-decision model, arguing Islamic cultural, religious, and personal values should be explicitly incorporated into the informed-consent process rather than treated as an obstacle to a Western autonomy-only model.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Directly positions T-PHE's shura (consultation) safeguard: argues informed consent in Muslim contexts is properly a shared, value-inclusive process rather than a purely individual autonomy transaction — foundational conceptual support for T-PHE's consent architecture, though it is a narrative argument, not empirical evidence of outcomes.
records.evidence_level: Tier one under the search brief's explicit carve-out for PubMed-indexed FIMA/IMANA-affiliated guideline-adjacent literature (Journal of IMA is IMANA's official journal); not a flagship general-medicine journal on its own merits.

records.title: The muslim physician and the ethics of medicine.
records.journal: The Journal of IMA (Islamic Medical Association of North America)
records.design: Conceptual/normative ethics essay
records.population_setting: Muslim physicians generally; no empirical cohort
records.key_finding: Argues that a Muslim physician guided by Qur'an and Sunna will embody the character traits of a trustworthy physician (compassion, honesty, accountability) and that this character-based grounding aligns with, rather than contradicts, Western-articulated principles of medical professionalism.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Directly positions amanah (entrusted responsibility/trustworthiness) as the organizing virtue of Muslim physician professionalism, explicitly linked to community trust — core conceptual grounding for T-PHE's professional-ethics term, supporting the pairing of Islamic virtue ethics with mainstream medical professionalism language.
records.evidence_level: Tier one under the search brief's explicit carve-out for PubMed-indexed FIMA/IMANA-affiliated literature (Journal of IMA is IMANA's official journal).

records.title: Considering Islamic Frameworks to Infectious Disease Prevention.
records.design: Narrative review
records.population_setting: Muslim-majority countries and communities; infectious-disease burden (dengue, cholera, malaria, COVID-19)
records.key_finding: Reviews how Islamic religious concepts (e.g., obligatory hygiene practices, communal responsibility) could be leveraged as public-health prevention frameworks in Muslim-majority settings facing high infectious-disease burden compounded by socioeconomic disparity, urbanization, and conflict.
records.relevance_to_tphe: Supports the broader analogy that Islamic religious concepts can be operationalized as public-health frameworks (an amanah/communal-responsibility argument) beyond the narrow bioethics literature — relevant as precedent for T-PHE's approach of translating an Islamic ethical vocabulary into a health-education programme design, though the clinical domain (infectious disease, not premarital/reproductive health) is distant and this should be cited only as a structural analogy.
records.evidence_level: Tier one — narrative review in Open Forum Infectious Diseases, an IDSA-affiliated peer-reviewed specialty journal (Oxford University Press), meeting the 'leading specialty journal' criterion.

gaps_noted: No PubMed-indexed hit for 'shura' (consultation) as an explicit named construct paired with clinical decision-making outside the informed-consent/shared-decision-making literature already captured; the term itself is undertheorized in the indexed medical-ethics literature relative to autonomy/beneficence.

No PubMed-indexed FIMA (Fiqh Council/Federation of Islamic Medical Associations) or IMANA formal position/guideline paper on premarital counseling, marriage preparation, or reproductive-decision consent was found (Q7 'FIMA/IMANA + guideline' returned 0 hits); the two Journal of IMA articles included (PMID 23610513, 23864762) are topical essays, not formal guidelines.

'Maslaha' (public interest/welfare) as an explicit named bioethical framework appears in the indexed literature (e.g., a 2024 Journal of Religion and Health paper, 'A Framework for Examining Bioethical Issues from a Sunni Perspective: Maslaha', PMID 36648579) but was excluded here because it is not a systematic review/meta-analysis and Journal of Religion and Health was restricted to SR/MA-tier records under the search brief's hard rule; flagging it as a known, indexed, but excluded-by-tier source the T-PHE team may still want to consult for conceptual (not evidence-tier) framing.

No PubMed-indexed record specifically evaluates premarital health education content (not screening, not marriage-age demography) delivered through an explicitly named Islamic ethical frame (faqr/taqwa/amanah/'adl/shura) in a Thai or Southeast Asian Muslim population — the closest analogues found (Bangladesh mosque-based diabetes RCT, PMID 41114978; Somali refugee mosque-based trauma RCT, PMID 39186273) are faith-integrated but not premarital-content trials, and are geographically/culturally distant from Thailand's Muslim minority context.

No BMC Medical Ethics systematic review specific to Islamic bioethics was found; the one Islamic-adjacent BMC Medical Ethics record located (PMID 41491519, a scoping review on social egg freezing) was excluded as insufficiently on-topic (not focused on a Muslim population or the five named ethical terms).
limits_of_this_search: This search covers only PubMed-indexed literature retrieved via NCBI E-utilities across 17 queries run 2026-09-02; it is not a formal systematic review (no dual-reviewer screening, no PRISMA flow, no grey literature, no fiqh-council primary-source jurisprudence search, no hand-search of FIMA/IMANA proceedings). Several included records are used as structural or population analogies (e.g., mainland-China religiosity SR, ultra-Orthodox Jewish HPV decision-aid study, Iran/Iraq/Uzbekistan self-immolation SR) rather than direct Muslim-Thai evidence, and are labeled as such in relevance_to_tphe. This search establishes that a citable tier-one Islamic medical-ethics and Muslim-health literature exists to pair with T-PHE's declared ethical frame; it does not, and must not be read to, establish that T-PHE itself is effective, validated, or endorsed by any of the cited sources.
